situationBrief.title: A Torn Noticeboard at School
situationBrief.description: A gust of wind blew across the school courtyard and scattered the noticeboard cards. Help Mira, Arjun, and Śukaji put every message back together.

storyIntro.sceneTitle: A Gust of Wind in the School Courtyard

beats.speaker: mira
beats.dialogue: Oh no! The afternoon breeze blew our school noticeboard cards across the courtyard. Each strip only makes half a thought.

beats.speaker: arjun
beats.dialogue: Look at the card I picked up—it just says '... plays cricket.' Who plays cricket? Something important is missing!

beats.speaker: shuka
beats.dialogue: Every complete message needs two parts working together: a Subject (who we talk about) and a Predicate (what is said about them). Let us repair them!

grammarOutcomes: Identify who or what a sentence is about (the Subject) and its core head-noun.
Identify what is said about the Subject (the Predicate, containing the finite verb).
See how Subject and Predicate join together to repair incomplete messages.
learningObjectives.knowledgeOutcome: Explore Indian school life, sports, and healthy nutrition through complete sentences.

sourceReferences.bookTitle: LEARN AND PRACTISE GRAMMAR CLASS - IX
sourceReferences.chapter: Chapter 1: Parts of a Sentence (Sections A & B)
sourceReferences.note: Teaches meaningful word order, Subject and Predicate, single-word vs multi-word Subjects, head-words, and understood 'you' in imperatives.

sourceReferences.bookTitle: A NEW METHOD English Grammar For Class IX & X

sourceReferences.bookTitle: A Practice Book of ENGLISH GRAMMAR & COMPOSITION (GRAMMAR IN USE) for Class IX

Original school story, courtyard examples, and interactive word-tile tasks built upon the cited textbook rules.

sentences.title: Starter Sentence
sentences.note: Primary demonstration sentence showing a three-word Subject and a two-word Predicate.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Points to one specific boy we have in mind.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Introduces the noun 'boy' inside the Subject.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Describes the boy by telling us he is small or young.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Modifies the head-noun 'boy' inside the Subject.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the person doing the action.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: This is the head-word of the Subject. The whole Subject is 'The little boy'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Shows the action happening.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: The finite verb starts the Predicate and matches the singular subject 'boy'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the game that the boy plays.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Completes the verb 'plays' as part of the Predicate 'plays cricket'.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'The little boy' names who the sentence is about.
groups.textbookRule: The part of a sentence that names the person or thing we speak about is called the Subject (Odisha Class IX, Ch. 1, p. 5; Assam Class IX-X, Ch. 1, p. 2).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.questionPrompt: What is said about the subject?
groups.plainExplanation: 'plays cricket' tells us what the little boy does.
groups.textbookRule: The part that says something about the Subject, containing the finite verb, is called the Predicate (Odisha Class IX, Ch. 1, p. 5; Assam Class IX-X, Ch. 1, p. 3).

relationships.label: Determiner → Noun
relationships.explanation: 'The' points to the noun 'boy', keeping them together inside the Subject.

relationships.label: Adjective → Noun
relationships.explanation: 'little' describes 'boy'. Describing words stay with their noun in the Subject.

relationships.label: Subject ↔ Verb
relationships.explanation: The verb 'plays' links directly to the Subject head-noun 'boy' and starts the Predicate.

sentences.title: Explore Sentence
sentences.note: Guided discovery sentence where students spot the Subject and the two-word verb Predicate before seeing the explanation.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Points to the specific group of students.
Names the learners performing the action.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Plural head-noun of the Subject 'The students'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Helping verb showing the reading is happening now.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Begins the Predicate 'are reading books' right after the Subject.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Shows the action the students are doing.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Main verb working with 'are' inside the Predicate.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names what the students are reading.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: 'The students' tells us who the sentence is about.
groups.textbookRule: A Subject names the people or things we speak about (Odisha Class IX, Ch. 1, p. 5).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.questionPrompt: What is said about the students?
groups.plainExplanation: 'are reading books' begins at the verb 'are' and tells what they are doing.
groups.textbookRule: Everything from the verb phrase onward telling about the Subject belongs to the Predicate (Odisha Class IX, Ch. 1, p. 5; Assam Class IX-X, Ch. 1, p. 3).

relationships.label: Subject ↔ Verb
relationships.explanation: Plural 'students' agrees with 'are reading', where the Predicate begins.

sentences.title: Comparison Sentence
sentences.rawText: The tall girl from Odisha eats fresh mangoes.
sentences.note: Shows how a prepositional phrase ('from Odisha') stays inside the Subject while 'girl' remains the head-word.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Points to one specific girl.
Describes the girl's height.
Names who the sentence is about.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Head-word of the five-word Subject 'The tall girl from Odisha'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Connects the girl to her home state.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Starts the phrase 'from Odisha', which tells us more about the girl inside the Subject.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the Indian state she comes from.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Completes the phrase 'from Odisha' inside the Subject.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Tells what the girl does.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Main verb starting the Predicate 'eats fresh mangoes'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Describes the mangoes as ripe and wholesome.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Adjective describing the noun 'mangoes' inside the Predicate.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the healthy fruit she eats.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Completes the Predicate after the verb 'eats'.

groups.label: Subject
groups.plainExplanation: All five words 'The tall girl from Odisha' tell us who the sentence is about.
groups.textbookRule: A Subject can be a multi-word noun group containing modifiers before or after the head-noun (Odisha Class IX, Ch. 1, pp. 5-6; Assam Class IX-X, Ch. 1, pp. 4-6).

groups.label: Predicate
groups.questionPrompt: What is said about the girl?
groups.plainExplanation: 'eats fresh mangoes' tells us what she does.
groups.textbookRule: Everything from the finite verb onward that tells us about the Subject forms the Predicate (Odisha Class IX, Ch. 1, p. 6).

relationships.label: Preposition phrase → Noun
relationships.explanation: 'from Odisha' describes 'girl', so it stays inside the Subject before the verb begins.

relationships.label: Subject Head ↔ Verb
relationships.explanation: 'eats' connects to the Subject head-word 'girl', even with 'from Odisha' in between.

structureSummary.patternNote: Longer Subject with 'from Odisha' + Predicate starting at the verb 'eats'

teachingSequence.title: Understand the Complete Sentence
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Words join in the right order to express one clear thought.
teachingSequence.explanation: 'The little boy plays cricket.' is a complete sentence. Tap any word to see its meaning and role.

teachingSequence.title: Discover the Subject
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Ask: Who are we talking about?
teachingSequence.explanation: 'The little boy' names who the sentence is about. Tap words or use the Subject control to inspect the group.

visualCallout.question: Who are we talking about?
visualCallout.label: 'The little boy' (head-noun: 'boy')
visualCallout.detail: 'The' and 'little' point to 'boy', answering who plays cricket. Without this Subject, the message feels unfinished.

teachingSequence.title: Understand the Subject's Meaning
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: The Subject names the person or thing performing or receiving the focus.
teachingSequence.explanation: 'boy' is the Subject head-noun; 'The' and 'little' stay attached to it so the listener knows exactly who is meant.

teachingSequence.title: Discover the Predicate
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Ask: What is said about the little boy?
teachingSequence.explanation: 'plays cricket' is the Predicate. It always contains the verb ('plays') and tells us what the Subject does.

teachingSequence.title: Understand the Complete Structure
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Subject + Predicate snap together to repair the notice.
teachingSequence.explanation: On the school noticeboard, 'The little boy' (Subject) + 'plays cricket' (Predicate) form one complete simple sentence.

guidedChallenge.promptSubject: Step 1: Tap the Subject in 'The students are reading books.'
guidedChallenge.promptPredicate: Step 2: Now tap the Predicate (starts at the verb 'are').
guidedChallenge.subjectFeedback: Ask 'Who are we talking about?' before the verb 'are'. Tap 'The' and 'students'.
guidedChallenge.predicateFeedback: Include all words from the helping verb 'are' onward: 'are', 'reading', and 'books'.
guidedChallenge.unlockedExplanation: Great work! 'The students' is the Subject (who), and 'are reading books' is the Predicate (what they are doing).

teachingSequence.title: Explore Another Example
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Find the Subject and Predicate first to unlock the explanation.
teachingSequence.explanation: Test the same two questions on 'The students are reading books.' before opening the full structure.

teachingSequence.title: Longer Subjects & Word Links
teachingSequence.shortPrompt: Even longer Subjects stop right before the finite verb.
teachingSequence.explanation: Compare both sentences: in 'The tall girl from Odisha eats fresh mangoes.', 'from Odisha' stays inside the Subject before 'eats'.

wordLabActivities.title: A. Identify Subject & Predicate
wordLabActivities.instruction: First tap every word in the Subject, then tap every word in the Predicate.

sentence.title: Noticeboard Sentence
sentence.rawText: Fresh vegetables from the garden keep us strong.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Describes the vegetables.
Names what the sentence is about.
Links vegetables to where they grow.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Part of the Subject phrase 'from the garden'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Points to the garden.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Inside the Subject modifier 'from the garden'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names where the vegetables come from.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Completes the Subject modifier before the verb 'keep'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Action/state verb starting the Predicate.
Refers to the people who stay strong.
Describes the result.

wordLabActivities.correctFeedback: Well done! 'Fresh vegetables from the garden' is the Subject, and 'keep us strong' is the Predicate.
wordLabActivities.incorrectSubjectFeedback: Check where the verb 'keep' begins. Everything describing the vegetables ('Fresh vegetables from the garden') belongs to the Subject.
wordLabActivities.incorrectPredicateFeedback: Select all words from the verb 'keep' through 'strong.' to complete the Predicate.
wordLabActivities.hint: Find the main verb ('keep') first. Everything before it is the Subject; everything from 'keep' onward is the Predicate.

wordLabActivities.title: B. Sort Subject & Predicate Cards
wordLabActivities.instruction: Tap a phrase card and place it into Subject (Who/What) or Predicate (What is said).

categories.label: Subject
categories.helperText: Who or what the sentence is about

categories.label: Predicate
categories.helperText: Starts with the verb; tells what happens

items.explanation: 'The school cricket team' names who we are talking about (noun group, no verb).
items.hint: Ask who the sentence is about — there is no verb here.

items.explanation: Starts with the verb 'drinks' and tells what the team does.
items.hint: Spot the action word 'drinks' right at the start.

items.explanation: Names the healthy foods being talked about.
items.hint: Names two healthy foods — there is no action verb yet.

items.explanation: Starts with the verb 'provide' and explains what they do.
items.hint: Begins with the verb 'provide' telling what the foods do.

wordLabActivities.completeFeedback: Great sorting! Notice how every Subject names a person or thing, while every Predicate begins with a verb.

wordLabActivities.title: C. Arrange Word Tiles
wordLabActivities.instruction: Tap the scrambled word tiles in order to repair this health notice.
wordLabActivities.promptContext: Hint: Put the Subject first, followed by the Predicate.
wordLabActivities.correctFeedback: Perfect! 'Children' (Subject) + 'drink clean water.' (Predicate) creates a clear, meaningful sentence.
wordLabActivities.incorrectFeedback: Put who the sentence is about first ('Children'), then the verb ('drink') and what they drink ('clean water.').

wordLabActivities.title: D. Swap Words & Observe Shift
wordLabActivities.instruction: Replace the adjective 'little' in 'The little boy plays cricket.' and see how the Subject's meaning shifts.

options.meaningEffect: Describes a small or young boy.
options.roleImpactNote: Still an adjective inside the Subject 'The little boy'.

options.meaningEffect: Changes the picture to a boy of greater height, while keeping the same Predicate 'plays cricket'.
options.roleImpactNote: Remains an adjective modifying the head-noun 'boy'.

options.meaningEffect: Highlights the boy's concentration during the game.
options.roleImpactNote: Remains an adjective inside the Subject; 'boy' is still the head-word.

wordLabActivities.takeaway: Swapping an adjective inside the Subject changes the description, while the Subject–Predicate structure stays intact.

wordLabActivities.title: E. Repair the Torn Notice
wordLabActivities.instruction: Choose the missing Predicate that turns this Subject into a complete sentence.

options.feedback: This tells where the library is, but has no finite verb—so the sentence is still incomplete.
Correct! 'opens at nine every morning' starts with the verb 'opens' and completes the Predicate.

options.text: hundreds of science and story books
options.feedback: This is only a noun group without a verb. A Predicate needs a verb like 'holds' or 'opens'.

wordLabActivities.title: F. Fix the Broken Message
wordLabActivities.instruction: Read the noticeboard strip below and identify why it is not a complete sentence.
wordLabActivities.brokenSentence: Fresh ripe bananas in the yellow basket.
wordLabActivities.repairedSentence: Fresh ripe bananas in the yellow basket taste sweet and healthy.
wordLabActivities.question: What is missing from 'Fresh ripe bananas in the yellow basket.'?

options.label: It has no Subject.
options.feedback: Actually, 'Fresh ripe bananas in the yellow basket' IS a Subject—we know what it names.

options.label: It has no Predicate (no verb telling us what happens).
options.feedback: Spot on! There is no verb telling us anything about the bananas. Adding 'taste sweet and healthy' supplies the Predicate.

options.label: It has too many nouns.
options.feedback: Having nouns like 'bananas' and 'basket' is fine inside a Subject phrase. The real gap is the missing verb and Predicate.

independentPractice.cueText: Light cue: Notice the two foods joined by 'and' before the verb 'give'.
independentPractice.title: Healthy Morning Notice
independentPractice.instruction: Identify the Subject first, then select the Predicate.

sentence.title: Independent Sentence 1
sentence.rawText: Warm milk and curd give steady energy.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Describes the milk.
Names the first nutritious food.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Part of the compound Subject 'Warm milk and curd'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Joins 'Warm milk' with 'curd'.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Connects the two nouns inside one Subject.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Names the second nutritious food.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Completes the compound Subject before the verb 'give'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Shows what milk and curd do.
Describes the lasting kind of energy.
Names what the foods provide.

independentPractice.successFeedback: Spot on! 'Warm milk and curd' is a compound Subject naming what we talk about, and 'give steady energy' is the Predicate.
independentPractice.retrySubjectFeedback: All four words 'Warm milk and curd' together form the Subject before the verb 'give'.
independentPractice.retryPredicateFeedback: Start at the verb 'give' and select every word through 'energy.'.

independentPractice.cueText: Find the linking verb ('is') to mark where the Predicate begins.
independentPractice.title: Drinking Water Notice
independentPractice.instruction: Tap all words in the Subject, then all words in the Predicate.

sentence.title: Independent Sentence 2
sentence.rawText: Clean water in covered pots is safe for everyone.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Describes the water.
Main noun naming what the notice is about.
Shows where the water is kept.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Starts the Subject modifier 'in covered pots'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Describes the pots.
Names the containers holding the water.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Ends the Subject before the verb 'is'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Connects the water to how safe it is.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Starts the Predicate 'is safe for everyone'.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Tells the condition of the water.
Connects 'safe' to who benefits.
Refers to all students and teachers.

independentPractice.successFeedback: Well done! 'in covered pots' describes 'water', so all five words form the Subject, and 'is safe for everyone' is the Predicate.
independentPractice.retrySubjectFeedback: Notice 'in covered pots' tells which water we mean—keep it inside the Subject and stop right before 'is'.
independentPractice.retryPredicateFeedback: The Predicate starts at the linking verb 'is' and runs to 'everyone.'.

independentPractice.title: Harvest Story Card
independentPractice.instruction: On your own: identify the Subject first, then the Predicate.

sentence.title: Independent Sentence 3
sentence.rawText: The young farmer from Assam grows sweet bananas.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Points to one farmer.
Describes the farmer.
Names the person we are talking about.
Connects the farmer to Assam.
Names the state in northeast India.
Shows what the farmer does.
Describes the bananas.
Names the healthy fruit grown.

independentPractice.successFeedback: Excellent! 'The young farmer from Assam' is the full Subject, and 'grows sweet bananas' is the Predicate.
independentPractice.retrySubjectFeedback: Ask 'Who grows sweet bananas?' Include 'from Assam' inside the Subject.
independentPractice.retryPredicateFeedback: Select everything from the verb 'grows' to 'bananas.'.

independentPractice.title: Courtyard Rule Notice
independentPractice.instruction: Read this school instruction card carefully and choose the true grammar rule.

sentence.title: Imperative Notice
sentence.rawText: Keep the school courtyard clean every day.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Gives a polite instruction.
tokens.grammaticalRoleExplanation: Starts the Predicate directly when 'You' is understood.

tokens.meaningInSentence: Points to the school courtyard.
Specifies which courtyard.
Names the open space at school.
Shows the condition to maintain.
Shows daily frequency.
Completes 'every day'.

structureSummary.predicateText: Keep the school courtyard clean every day

independentPractice.imperativeQuestion: In this command sentence, where is the Subject?

imperativeOptions.label: 'Keep' is the Subject because it comes first.
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'Keep' is an action verb, so it starts the Predicate—even though it stands first in a command.

imperativeOptions.label: The Subject is the understood '(You)', and the whole spoken line is the Predicate.
imperativeOptions.feedback: Correct! In imperative sentences, '(You)' is understood as the Subject, and the whole command forms the Predicate.

imperativeOptions.label: 'courtyard' is the Subject.
imperativeOptions.feedback: 'the school courtyard' is what you keep clean (the Object inside the Predicate), not the person given the instruction.

independentPractice.successFeedback: Great work! You spotted the understood '(You)' Subject in an imperative notice.

completionSummary.headline: The Noticeboard Is Restored!
completionSummary.celebrationMessage: Mira, Arjun, and Śukaji pinned every repaired sentence back onto the courtyard noticeboard. All school messages are clear again!
learnedPoints: A complete sentence expresses one clear thought using a Subject and a Predicate.
The Subject names who or what we are talking about, centred on its head-noun (or understood 'You' in commands).
The Predicate tells us something about the Subject and always contains the finite verb.
repairedMessages: Fresh ripe bananas in the yellow basket taste sweet and healthy.
Keep the school courtyard clean every day.
completionSummary.rewardLabel: Noticeboard Restorer Star & Fresh Fruit Basket
